facts.value: Paragraph 36 (PDF p.9) prints £53,000k of long-term borrowing at 3.64% weighted, plus a £500k temporary loan from Portchester Crematorium Joint Committee at 2.09%, totalling £53,500k. Our PWLB price book at 31 March 2026 shows 14 loans totalling £53,000,000 at a weighted 3.6235%. The £53,000k long-term line ties to our file to the pound; weighted rates agree to within 0.02 percentage points (rounding).

source.title: Capital and Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 — Executive, 6 July 2026

facts.note: Portchester Crematorium £500k line is a temp loan FROM the Portchester Crematorium Joint Committee to Fareham (para 37), not PWLB — correctly absent from our book. Our 14 loans therefore represent 100% of Fareham's long-term PWLB position. Profile mix: 12 MATURITY + 2 EIP. Maturity ladder: 2 loans at 2-5y (£7.0m, 4.18%), 1 loan at 5-10y (£2.8m, 3.75%), 1 loan at 10-25y (£3.2m, 3.82%), 10 loans at 25+y (£40.0m, 3.50%). The 25+ bucket is ten identical £4m maturity loans running to 30 September 2058-2061 at 3.48-3.50% — consistent with the £49.3m HRA self-financing debt from 2012 the paper cites at Appendix C p.21.

facts.value: Total CFR £125,600k (31.03.25 Actual) → £118,992k (31.03.26 Actual), movement (£6,608k). Split at 31.03.26: GF CFR £58,827k, HRA CFR £60,165k. Total borrowing £61,836k → £53,500k. Under Borrowing (internal borrowing) £65,492k at 31.03.26. Balance-sheet identity ties: CFR £118,992 − External £53,500 − OLTL £0 = Internal £65,492, matching the paper's print at Appendix C p.20.

source.title: Capital and Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 — Executive, 6 July 2026

facts.note: Appendix C p.19 (CFR table) and p.20 (Gross Debt vs CFR table). Paper's Under/Over Borrowing print £65,492k for 2025/26 Actual matches the identity to the pound. HRA CFR essentially flat (£60,172k → £60,165k, -£7k) — no HRA borrowing in year (para 40). GF CFR fell £6,601k (65,428 → 58,827) as capex financed by debt was lower than anticipated and lower than MRP + capital receipts (paper narrative Appendix C p.19).

facts.value: Internal borrowing (Under Borrowing) £65,492k at 31 March 2026, up from £63,764k a year earlier (£125,600 − £61,836 − 0). 55.0% of CFR is currently funded from the Council's own cash/reserves. Investments held £21,747k against internal borrowing of £65,492k — a c.£43.7m capacity for further externalisation if desired.

source.title: Capital and Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 — Executive, 6 July 2026

facts.note: Fareham runs a heavy internal-borrowing position — 55% of CFR unfunded externally is at the higher end of the library. Para 38 confirms the strategy: 'the Council's main objective when borrowing has been to strike an appropriately low risk balance between securing lower interest costs and achieving cost certainty over the period for which funds are required, with flexibility to renegotiate loans should the Council's long-term plans change, being a secondary objective.'

facts.value: Loans maturing within 1 year: 1% actual against a 50% upper limit (Appendix C p.21). 1-2 years 0%; 2-5 years 13%; 5-10 years 11%; over 10 years 75% against a 100% upper limit. Only c.1% (~£530k) of the book reprices in a year; only c.14% (~£7.4m) reprices inside five years. The book is unusually long-dated for a district — 75% sits beyond 10 years.

source.title: Capital and Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 — Executive, 6 July 2026

facts.note: Applied to £53,000k the paper's 75% >10-year share (~£39.75m) agrees with our engine's 25+ years bucket of £40.0m to within £250k. The paper uses a two-tier over-10 grouping; our engine splits it into 10-25 and 25+ separately. Ten identical £4m maturity loans running to 2058-2061 at 3.48-3.50% dominate the book — HRA self-financing debt from 2012.

facts.value: HRA debt £58,300k at 31.03.26 (down £5,000k from Revised £63,300k). 2,370 dwellings. Debt-to-revenues ratio 3.61:1 (Revised 3.95:1). Debt per dwelling £24,599 (Revised £26,655). Debt Repayment Fund £7,340k held. HRA CFR £60,165k — matches Appendix C p.19.

source.title: Capital and Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 — Executive, 6 July 2026

facts.note: Appendix C p.21 HRA Ratios table. Debt-to-Revenues 3.61 is a moderate/low HRA leverage — well below the 5-6 range seen at heavier HRA borrowers. Paper text: 'the Council moved from a subsidy system to self-financing and was required to take on £49.3 million of debt. In addition, the HRA has taken on £9 million of debt to finance capital expenditure.' Consistent with our engine's £40m in 10 identical £4m loans at 3.48-3.50% dating to 2012.

facts.value: Para 40 (PDF p.9): 'A Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) HRA rate which is 0.4% below the certainty rate is available up to March 2027. This discounted rate is to support local authorities borrowing for the Housing Revenue Account providing a window of opportunity for HRA-related borrowing. No HRA borrowing was required in 2025/26 but is set to increase by £4.4 million in 2026/27 for new build capital projects.'

source.title: Capital and Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 — Executive, 6 July 2026

facts.note: Two dated forward-looking commitments in a single paragraph: (i) the March 2027 sunset of the 0.4% HRA rate concession; (ii) planned £4.4m HRA borrowing in 2026/27. Both self-published. The HRA rate is priced daily on pwlbtoday.org — a natural training/product angle.

facts.value: Operational Boundary £145,000k (2025/26 Revised); Authorised Limit £155,000k. Actual debt £53,500k at 31.03.26. Both complied (Appendix C p.20). Debt sits £91,500k below Operational Boundary and £101,500k below Authorised Limit — very substantial headroom against declared limits.

source.title: Capital and Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 — Executive, 6 July 2026

facts.note: The Operational Boundary at 2.7× actual debt is very generous — consistent with the internal-borrowing strategy leaving headroom for potential externalisation. Not an outreach topic; recorded for the file.

officer.body:
Hi,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's premature-repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the Capital and Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26 that went to the Executive on 6 July. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it. It's a clear report and this is offered in that spirit, not as a critique.

A reconciliation first. Paragraph 36 prints £53,000k of long-term borrowing at a weighted 3.64% (plus the £500k temporary loan from Portchester Crematorium Joint Committee, which sits outside PWLB). Our PWLB file at 31 March 2026 holds 14 loans totalling £53,000,000 at a weighted 3.6235%. That ties to the pound on principal, and the 0.02 percentage-point gap on rate is just rounding. Balance-sheet identity ties too: your CFR of 118,992 less external borrowing 53,500 less other long-term liabilities zero equals internal borrowing 65,492, which is exactly what Appendix C prints as Under Borrowing.

What's most distinctive in the file is the shape of the book and what it's worth today. Ten identical £4m maturity loans running to 30 September 2058-2061 at 3.48-3.50% account for £40m of the £53m — the HRA self-financing debt Appendix C traces back to 2012. That leaves the book with 75% beyond ten years and only about 1% repricing within a year. Priced against today's certainty curve (14 August, notice 314/26 PM) our engine values the 14 live loans about £12.16m below par indicatively — 23% of principal — with 13 of the 14 loans sitting below par. The discount is spread almost evenly across the ten long-dated loans; the four with the latest maturities show roughly £1.23-1.27m each and the other six sit not far behind. That is what borrowing at 3.5% locks in against a 5.83% ten-year certainty curve today. Every council's book is priced daily on this basis at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis — same engine, same DMO curve. Indicative only, of course; only the DMO can quote, and we model no MRP or accounting treatment on top.

Paragraph 40 flags something else worth putting side by side. The 0.4% HRA rate concession is available until March 2027, and you're planning £4.4m of HRA borrowing in 2026/27 for new build. That would drop into the same maturity space where your existing book already sits at 3.5% — so the comparison to make when the moment comes is not to a rate-book average but to the marginal HRA rate on the day. The HRA rate is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/dashboard alongside the standard and certainty curves. If Bank Rate stays around Arlingclose's central 3.75% view for the rest of the concession window, the working-out is: how much of the £4.4m draws before end-March 2027 to catch the 40bp, and whether laddering it (or drawing in one lump) matters against maturity buckets already at 75% above ten years.

A small piece of wider context. July's sector PWLB drawings across all councils were £368m from just 19 borrowers — a thin month — and the breakdown by tenor and council is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity. It gives a sense of what shape of borrowing has actually been going through since the outturn was set. On our side we hold PWLB only, so the £500k Portchester Crematorium temp loan and any market or bank debt outside PWLB sit outside our file.

Four courses fit. Reading the PWLB certainty curve covers the mechanics of what your paper references at paragraph 40. Liability Benchmark: the essentials is worth watching given where CIPFA is heading with the Prudential and Treasury Code updates — Fareham runs 55% of CFR internally, and the LB is the tool that dates the horizon on that. IFRS 9 statutory override — the 2029 cliff matters given the £10.75m of pooled fund holdings inside the override at Appendix C, and your own paragraph 45 flags that the government may still change it. And Members' introduction to treasury is the one to point Executive members at ahead of the next strategy cycle. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Sources: Capital and Treasury Management Outturn 2025/26, Executive, 6 July 2026 (moderngov.fareham.gov.uk/documents/s49536).
